title: The Capuchins (1528)
hook: a reform with hoods, beards and poverty; Padre Pio was one

segments.voice: Yesterday, the keepers of the Holy Land, and the walk they carried home to every parish wall. Your line was the custody. What small place did you take care of? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-three.

In old paintings of the saints, some friars look a little wilder than the rest: a full beard, a long pointed hood, bare feet in sandals, a habit of rough cloth patched where it wore through. The difference is on purpose. Inside the family of Francis, a group of brothers came to believe the order had drifted from the poverty he loved. They wanted to go back. Back to hermitages and begging, to preaching in plain words to plain people. They took up a hood shaped the way they believed Francis wore his, and people gave them a nickname for it. Today's word is that nickname.
screen: `A BEARD, A HOOD, BARE FEET.` → `THE ORDER HAD DRIFTED.` → `GO BACK TO FRANCIS.`

segments.voice: Capuchin. Tradition says the name comes from the Italian word for that hood. The friars didn't choose it; the street did. And it stuck. What they wanted was simple and hard: to live the Rule of Francis without the comforts that had crept in. Smaller houses. Fewer things. Long hours of prayer in silence, and then out among ordinary people. The early years were not easy. The reform had opponents inside the Franciscan family, and for a time it was not clear it would survive. It did, and it stayed within the family: Capuchins are Franciscans, one branch of the same tree, following the same Rule. Tradition remembers them for staying when sickness came to a town, nursing the dying when others fled. And then there is a Capuchin friar in southern Italy, Padre Pio, whom the Church now honors as Saint Pio of Pietrelcina. People traveled from far away to bring him their confessions and stood in long lines to do it. There were reports that he bore wounds like the wounds of Christ, and the Church looked into those reports with care and caution. What drew people, though, was often simpler. Here was a poor friar in a brown hood who would listen to the worst thing you had done. It echoes the invitation of Jesus in Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "Come to me, all you that labour, and are burdened, and I will refresh you." A hood, a beard, a confessional. The reform kept pointing at the same thing: go back to the poor man of Assisi, and then go out.
screen: `A NICKNAME FROM THE STREET.` · `LIVE THE RULE WITHOUT THE COMFORTS.` · `STILL FRANCISCANS: ONE BRANCH, ONE TREE.` · `PADRE PIO AND THE LONG LINES.` · then, large: `AND I WILL REFRESH YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold the hooded friars in mind. Settle, and breathe. Picture one Capuchin somewhere today: in a soup line, in a hospital corridor, in a confessional with the little light on, waiting for whoever comes. You won't know his name. Now bring to mind someone in your own life who listens to other people's burdens for a living, a nurse, a counselor, a priest, a friend everyone calls. If you pray, you can pray for the Capuchins and for that person, in your own words or with an Our Father. If you don't, just hold them both kindly for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Capuchin. A Franciscan reform that went back to poverty and prayer, named, tradition says, for its hood. Padre Pio wore it. Today's word.
Your line: the hooded friars. Today, when someone starts to tell you something heavy, put down what you're holding and listen all the way to the end. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Capuchin friars live in community under the Rule of Saint Francis, and are often found in parishes, soup kitchens, hospitals and confessionals; Catholics who are devoted to Saint Pio of Pietrelcina often ask his prayers.

notes: Claims rule: the title's date (1528, Pope Clement VII's bull Religionis zelus) is not repeated in the voice. Founders (Matteo da Bascio and companions) are not named; confirm whether a Keeper wants them.
The derivation of 'Capuchin' from Italian cappuccio is attributed to tradition; also the folk link to the capuchin monkey and cappuccino ('some say'). Confirm.
'Tradition remembers them for staying when sickness came to a town' (Capuchin service in plague times) is stated generally; confirm.

Padre Pio: the voice says 'a Capuchin friar in southern Italy' and 'reports that he bore wounds like the wounds of Christ', which 'the Church looked into with care and caution'. Confirm the phrasing is fair to both devotion and the Church's investigations.
